indiaMissions.title: The St Thomas Christians of Kerala
indiaMissions.region: Kerala (the Malabar coast); historically also the Coromandel coast around Mylapore (Chennai)
indiaMissions.summary: The St Thomas Christians (Nasranis, Mar Thoma Nasranis) of Kerala trace their church to the apostle Thomas, said to have landed at Muziris in AD 52 and to have been killed near Mylapore around 72. The apostolic founding cannot be proved, but a Syriac-using church with bishops from the Church of the East is securely attested on the Malabar coast by the sixth century at the latest. For more than a thousand years the Nasranis lived as a high-status trading and landholding community woven into Kerala's caste society, “Hindu in culture, Christian in religion and Oriental in worship”, before Portuguese intervention split them into the many Syrian churches of today.
indiaMissions.story:
Kerala tradition holds that the apostle Thomas arrived at Muziris (Kodungallur) in AD 52, converted several Brahmin families and founded seven and a half churches: Kodungallur, Palayur, Kottakkavu (Paravur), Kokkamangalam, Niranam, Nilackal (Chayal), Kollam and the “half church” (Arappally) at Thiruvithamcode. He is said to have crossed to the Coromandel coast and been speared to death near Mylapore around 72. The earliest written account, the Syriac Acts of Thomas (Edessa, early third century), sends Thomas to the court of King Gondophares — a real Indo-Parthian ruler of the north-west, known from coins and the Takht-i-Bahi inscription — which shows that its author knew something genuine about first-century India. Church fathers from Ephrem to Jerome linked Thomas with India, and Eusebius reports that Pantaenus of Alexandria (c. 180) found Christians in “India”, although that word could also mean Arabia or Ethiopia. Busy Roman trade with Muziris, confirmed by the Muziris papyrus and the Pattanam excavations, makes an early mission plausible, but historians such as Stephen Neill and Robert Frykenberg conclude that it can be neither proved nor disproved. Kerala's own oral tradition, preserved in songs such as the Thomma Parvam (Ramban Pattu), was written down only in the early modern period.

Firmer ground comes with the Church of the East. The Alexandrian merchant Cosmas Indicopleustes (c. 550) reported Christians in “Male, where the pepper grows” and a bishop at Kalliana ordained in Persia. Community tradition dates a migration of some 72 Syrian Christian families under the merchant Thomas of Cana (Knai Thomman) to around 345; their descendants, the Knanaya or “Southists”, have kept strict endogamy ever since, distinct from the “Northist” majority. A second arrival of Persian clergy, Mar Sapor and Mar Prodh, at Kollam around 825 is remembered in the founding of churches, and the Tharisappalli copper plates of 849 confirm that a Christian merchant guild and church in Kollam enjoyed royal privileges. Bishops came from Mesopotamia and used the East Syriac liturgy of Addai and Mari; daily leadership lay with an Indian archdeacon (the Jathikku Karthavyan, “head of the community”).

The Nasranis were integrated into Kerala society as a high caste, ranked alongside the Nairs. Rulers granted them privileges such as riding elephants, using palanquins, carrying swords and collecting certain dues; they were prominent in the pepper trade and served as soldiers trained in kalari martial arts. They observed caste purity — avoiding contact with Pulaya and Paraya labourers — and many owned agrestic slaves until Travancore abolished slavery in 1855. Their churches resembled temples, with flagstaffs, lamps and processions; their marriage rites included the tali; and they shared festivals and customs with Hindu neighbours. The Carmelite historian Placid Podipara later summed this up in the formula “Hindu (Indian) in culture, Christian in religion and Oriental in worship”. The community was devout but not, for most of its history, outwardly missionary: it reproduced itself as a caste rather than seeking converts.

The arrival of Vasco da Gama in 1498 began a new era. Leaders of the community welcomed the Portuguese as fellow Christians and potential protectors, and in 1504 East Syriac bishops in Kerala wrote to their patriarch that there were some 30,000 Christian families in Malabar. Portuguese clergy soon treated Syriac practice as “Nestorian” heresy. Latinisation culminated in the Synod of Diamper (1599) and provoked the Coonan Cross Oath of 1653, which split the community into the Catholic Pazhayakoor (“old allegiance”) and the independent Puthenkoor (“new allegiance”), which in 1665 adopted the West Syriac (Antiochene) tradition (see the Diamper and Coonan Cross entry).

Further divisions followed. The Malabar Independent Syrian Church at Thozhiyur separated in 1772. Contact with the Church Missionary Society's “Mission of Help” (from 1816) inspired the reformer Abraham Malpan, whose movement became the Mar Thoma Syrian Church (separated by the Royal Court of Travancore ruling of 1889); evangelicals later left it to form the St Thomas Evangelical Church (1961). A group that sought renewed links with the East Syriac patriarch became the Chaldean Syrian Church of Thrissur. The Puthenkoor itself divided between the autocephalous Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church (catholicate 1912) and the Jacobite Syrian Christian Church loyal to the Syriac Orthodox patriarch of Antioch, a dispute over churches and property that went to India's Supreme Court in 1958, 1995 and 2017. In 1930 Mar Ivanios led part of the Orthodox into communion with Rome as the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church, while the Catholic Pazhayakoor received Indian bishops in 1896 and became the Syro-Malabar Catholic Church, a major-archiepiscopal church from 1992.

In the twentieth century the Syrian churches turned outward. The Mar Thoma Evangelistic Association (1888), the Syro-Malabar missionary congregations such as the Missionary Society of St Thomas (1968), and thousands of Kerala priests, nuns, nurses and teachers carried Kerala Christianity to north India, the Gulf and the West; in 2017 Rome gave the Syro-Malabar Church jurisdiction throughout India. Yet relations with Dalit converts brought into Syrian churches by nineteenth-century missions were often marked by separate congregations and discrimination, a grievance voiced sharply by Poykayil Yohannan, who left the Mar Thoma church to found the Prathyaksha Raksha Daiva Sabha in 1909. In the 2011 census Kerala had about 6.14 million Christians, 18.4 per cent of the state's population.

indiaMissions.legacy: The St Thomas Christians give Indian Christianity its claim to be as old as Christianity itself and not a colonial import. Their history also shows the cost of deep inculturation: a church thoroughly Indian in custom absorbed caste along with culture. Their fragmentation into eight or more churches under Portuguese, Syriac Orthodox, Anglican and Roman influences mirrors the wider history of world Christianity in a single Kerala community.

indiaMissions.title: Persian crosses, copper plates and the Church of the East in India
indiaMissions.region: Kerala (Kollam, Kodungallur, Kottayam), the Coromandel coast (Mylapore), the Konkan (Kalyan, Thane) and Sri Lanka

place.name: Kollam (Quilon), Kerala — site of the Tharisa church

indiaMissions.summary: From late antiquity until 1599 the Christians of India belonged to the Church of the East, whose patriarch sat at Seleucia-Ctesiphon and later Baghdad. Bishops, liturgy and Syriac learning came from Mesopotamia and Persia along the sea routes of the Indian Ocean trade. Their traces survive in Pahlavi-inscribed 'Persian crosses', the Tharisappalli copper plates of 849, travellers' reports from Cosmas to Marco Polo, and letters between Kerala and the patriarchs that end only with the Portuguese-enforced break at Diamper.
indiaMissions.story:
The Church of the East grew up in the Persian (Sasanian) empire, outside the Roman world and its councils, and was the great missionary church of Asia, reaching Central Asia and Tang China by 635. India lay at the end of its maritime networks. A bishop styled 'John the Persian, of all Persia and Great India' is listed among those at Nicaea in 325, though the title's meaning is debated. The first reliable witness is the Alexandrian merchant Cosmas Indicopleustes, who around 550 wrote that there were churches in Taprobane (Sri Lanka) served by Persian clergy, in “Male, where the pepper grows”, and at Kalliana (Kalyan near Mumbai), where a bishop was appointed from Persia.

India's place in the hierarchy changed over time. In the 650s the Catholicos Isho'yahb III rebuked the metropolitan of Fars, who claimed authority over India, for leaving the Indian churches without clergy. Under the great Catholicos Timothy I (780–823), India was organised as a metropolitan province of the 'exterior' provinces, whose metropolitan was required only to send a letter of communion every six years because of the distance. Syriac remained the language of liturgy and theology; Indian Christians used the East Syriac rite of Addai and Mari and called their bishops 'Mar'.

The richest documentary evidence is the set of copper plates known as the Tharisappalli or Quilon plates (c. 849). In them Ayyan Adikal Thiruvadikal, ruler of Venad under the Chera king Sthanu Ravi, granted land, serfs and trading rights to the church (palli) of Tharisa at Kollam, built by the merchant Maruvan Sapir Iso, and placed the church under the protection of the Anjuvannam and Manigramam merchant guilds. The plates are witnessed by eleven signatories in Arabic (Kufic), ten in Middle Persian (Pahlavi) and four in Judeo-Persian (Hebrew script) — vivid proof of a cosmopolitan Indian Ocean trading world. Later plates, such as the Iravi Korttan grant at Kodungallur (traditionally dated 1225; the date is debated), show Christian merchants holding guild titles. The so-called Persian crosses — granite slabs carved with a cross rising from a lotus beneath a dove and bearing Pahlavi inscriptions — have been found at St Thomas Mount near Chennai (unearthed by the Portuguese in 1547), in the Valiyapalli at Kottayam (two crosses), at Kadamattom, Muttuchira and Alangad in Kerala, at Agassaim in Goa (2001) and at Anuradhapura in Sri Lanka. Scholars date them between the seventh and tenth centuries; one common reading of the inscription asks the Lord Christ to have mercy on the man who made the cross.

Western visitors came intermittently. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records that King Alfred sent alms to St Thomas in India in 883, though the destination may be legendary. Marco Polo described the tomb of Thomas at Mylapore in about 1293. The Franciscan John of Montecorvino spent thirteen months there in 1291–92 on his way to China; the Dominican Jordanus Catalani was appointed Latin bishop of Columbum (Kollam) in 1329; and the papal legate Giovanni de' Marignolli worshipped at a Latin church in Kollam in 1348. These Latin contacts left little lasting trace, and the Indian church continued to look to Mesopotamia.

By the fifteenth century the Church of the East had been devastated in its homeland by plague, Timur's campaigns and decline, and India sometimes went decades without bishops. In 1490 Kerala sent three men to the Catholicos Shemon IV, who consecrated two monks, Mar Thomas and Mar John, for India. In 1503 Elijah V sent four more — Mar Yahballaha, Mar Denha, Mar Jacob and Mar Thomas — whose letter of 1504 reported about 30,000 Christian families and the newly arrived Portuguese. Mar Jacob (d. c. 1552) cooperated closely with the Portuguese at Cranganore. After the 1552 schism in Mesopotamia created a rival Chaldean patriarchate in communion with Rome, both lines sent bishops: Mar Joseph Sulaqa (d. 1569) and Mar Abraham (d. 1597), who manoeuvred between the patriarchs, Rome and the Portuguese. The Portuguese increasingly intercepted East Syriac bishops at sea. Mar Abraham's death in 1597 gave Archbishop Menezes of Goa the opportunity to end the connection at the Synod of Diamper in 1599. Thereafter only a small Chaldean Syrian Church in Thrissur (re-linked to the Assyrian patriarch from 1874 and organised under Mar Abimalek Timotheus from 1908) continued the East Syriac affiliation, while the Syro-Malabar Church kept the East Syriac rite in a Latinised form within the Catholic Church.

indiaMissions.legacy: The East Syriac connection shows that Indian Christianity was part of an Asian Christian world centred on Baghdad long before Europeans arrived. Its material remains — the Pahlavi crosses and multilingual copper plates — are among the best evidence for the cosmopolitan Indian Ocean of the ninth century, and its liturgical heritage became the focus of twentieth-century efforts to undo Latinisation.

indiaMissions.title: Portuguese Padroado, Goa and the Goa Inquisition
indiaMissions.region: Goa, the Konkan and Bombay–Bassein coast, Mangalore (Kanara), Cochin, and Portuguese enclaves on the Coromandel and Bengal coasts
indiaMissions.summary: Under the Padroado Real, papal bulls of the fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries gave the Portuguese crown the right and duty to fund, staff and govern the Catholic Church throughout its eastern empire. From the conquest of Goa in 1510 Portuguese India became a Catholic territory: temples were destroyed, Hindu rites restricted, orphans baptised, and from 1560 the Goa Inquisition policed converts until 1812. The same system produced India's first printing press, Konkani and Marathi Christian literature, a large Goan and Mangalorean Catholic community and a long jurisdictional quarrel with Rome.
indiaMissions.story:
The Padroado (patronage) grew out of papal bulls such as Romanus Pontifex (1455), Inter caetera (1456) and Praecelsae devotionis (1514), which granted the kings of Portugal control of church appointments and revenues in lands they 'discovered' in return for supporting missions. When Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498, and Afonso de Albuquerque captured Goa from the Sultan of Bijapur in 1510, church and empire advanced together. Franciscans accompanied the early fleets and opened a friary in Goa in 1517; Goa became a diocese in 1534 and an archdiocese, with the title 'Primate of the East', in 1558. Dominicans (1548), Jesuits (1542), Augustinians (1572) and later Carmelites and Theatines followed. Cochin (1558) and Cranganore became suffragan sees; the see of Mylapore (San Thome) was created in 1606.

In the 1540s the colonial state turned from tolerance to active Christianisation in its core territories of Tiswadi (Ilhas), Bardez and Salcete. Temples on the islands were ordered destroyed in 1540–41 and their lands transferred to churches and the Confraternity of the Holy Faith (1541); the College of St Paul trained boys of many Asian nations. Viceregal and conciliar decrees between 1559 and 1567 — including the 1559 law that Hindu children left fatherless were to be handed to the Jesuits for baptism, bans on public Hindu worship and festivals, the expulsion of Brahmin priests and preference in office for Christians — produced mass baptisms, often of entire villages following their headmen. Many Hindu families fled across the border, carrying their deities to new temples in Ponda and beyond. The First Provincial Council of Goa (1567) codified this policy. By the early seventeenth century the majority of the population of the 'Old Conquests' was Catholic, while caste survived among converts as Bamonn (Brahmin), Chardo (Kshatriya), Gauddo and Sudir groups.

Francis Xavier, writing to King João III in 1545, asked for an Inquisition; it was established in Goa in 1560. Its first target was New Christians — converted Jews and their descendants, such as the physician Garcia de Orta, whose remains were exhumed and burned in 1580 — but it increasingly prosecuted Hindu converts suspected of continuing ancestral rites, and even regulated Hindu practice in Portuguese lands. Contemporary and later accounts, notably the French physician Charles Dellon's narrative of his imprisonment (1687), made it notorious in Europe. Historians estimate that some 16,000 people were tried between 1561 and 1774, with dozens burned in person or in effigy. The Marquis of Pombal suppressed it in 1774; it was restored in 1778 and finally abolished in 1812, and most of its archive was destroyed.

The Padroado also sustained real cultural achievement. The first printing press in India was set up at the College of St Paul in 1556. The English Jesuit Thomas Stephens wrote a Konkani grammar and the Kristapurana (printed 1616), an epic retelling of the Bible in the Marathi-Konkani of Hindu puranic poetry; Jesuit and Franciscan scholars produced grammars, catechisms and dictionaries in Konkani, Marathi and Tamil. The Rachol Seminary (from 1610) trained Goan clergy, and Goan priests such as Joseph Vaz, who secretly rebuilt the Catholic church of Dutch-ruled Ceylon from 1687, became missionaries in their own right. Portuguese enclaves at Bassein, Chaul, Bombay, Daman, Diu, Mangalore, Nagapattinam and Hooghly left lasting Catholic communities such as the East Indians of Bombay and the Mangalorean Catholics.

The Padroado's claims soon collided with Rome. In 1622 the papacy founded the Congregation de Propaganda Fide to take direct control of missions, and from 1637 it appointed vicars apostolic in India — beginning with the Goan Brahmin Matheus de Castro, the first Indian bishop — in territories Portugal claimed but could no longer control. The resulting 'double jurisdiction' produced rival priests, excommunications and, in the nineteenth century, the 'Goan schism' after Pope Gregory XVI's brief Multa praeclare (1838) suppressed Padroado sees outside Portuguese territory. Concordats in 1857 and 1886 created a compromise hierarchy, and the Padroado in India was wound down after 1928 and ended after India annexed Goa in 1961. Meanwhile Mangalorean Catholics suffered captivity under Tipu Sultan, who deported tens of thousands to Seringapatam in 1784; many died before their release in 1799.

The Padroado's legacy is double-edged. It planted a large, culturally distinct Catholic population on India's west coast and supplied the subcontinent with priests, musicians, teachers and administrators. It also made Christianity in India look like the religion of the conqueror — 'Parangi' (Firangi) religion — associating it with temple destruction, forced baptism and inquisitorial terror, memories that Hindu nationalist writers have revived. In the 2011 census Goa's 366,130 Christians formed about 25 per cent of the state's population.

indiaMissions.title: Francis Xavier and the Paravars of the Pearl Fishery Coast
indiaMissions.region: The Fishery Coast of southern Tamil Nadu (Tuticorin to Kanyakumari) and the Mukkuvar coast of Travancore
indiaMissions.summary: In 1535–37 the Paravars, a Tamil caste of pearl-divers and fishers on the Gulf of Mannar, accepted mass baptism in return for Portuguese protection against Muslim rivals and inland overlords. From 1542 the Jesuit Francis Xavier gave this nominal conversion content, touring some thirty coastal villages with Tamil prayers, child catechists and village kanakkapillais, before baptising thousands of Mukkuvar fishers in Travancore. The result was the first Catholic caste community created by mission in India — durable, devout and fiercely loyal to its Catholic identity, but born of a political bargain.
indiaMissions.story:
The Paravars lived in some thirty villages along the coast from Tuticorin to Cape Comorin, earning their living from fishing and from the famous pearl beds of the Gulf of Mannar. In the early 1530s they were squeezed between Muslim Marakkayar traders, who competed for the pearl fishery with the backing of the Zamorin's fleets, and the Nayak overlords of the Vijayanagara empire inland. After a quarrel at Tuticorin around 1532, Paravar headmen sought help from the Portuguese at Cochin. The price of protection was baptism: between 1535 and 1537 the vicar-general Miguel Vaz and other priests baptised some 20,000 Paravars in a series of mass ceremonies. In 1538 a Portuguese fleet destroyed the Muslim flotilla at Vedalai, confirming the alliance — and a Portuguese share of the pearl fishery.

The converts received almost no instruction. When Francis Xavier — a Navarrese co-founder of the Society of Jesus sent east as papal nuncio — arrived in Goa on 6 May 1542, he was asked to go to the Fishery Coast, which he reached in October 1542 with two Tamil-speaking seminarians. With their help he had the Creed, the Ten Commandments, the Lord's Prayer, the Hail Mary and the Confiteor translated into Tamil, memorised them phonetically, and walked from village to village ringing a bell to gather boys and girls, who learned the prayers and taught them to their parents. He baptised infants, destroyed images, nursed the sick and appointed in each village a kanakkapillai (literate catechist-accountant) to lead prayers and teach on Sundays. In a letter of January 1544 he wrote that his arms were often too tired to baptise any more.

Xavier's work was bound up with Portuguese power and violence. He protested to the governor about Portuguese captains who oppressed the Paravars, but also relied on them. When Badaga raiders from the Vijayanagara overlords attacked the coast in 1544, he organised relief boats for refugees at Manapad. In late 1544, with the support of the Raja of Travancore, he moved to the Mukkuvar fishing villages south of Trivandrum, claiming to have baptised some 10,000 people in a single month. On Mannar island, the Raja of Jaffna, Cankili I, massacred several hundred new converts in 1544; Xavier's call for a punitive expedition was never carried out. Xavier left India for Mylapore and Malacca in 1545 and went on to the Moluccas and Japan, returning to India only briefly before he died on Shangchuan island off China in December 1552.

The Jesuits made the Fishery Coast a permanent mission. The Italian Antonio Criminali became the first Jesuit martyr when he was killed at Vedalai in 1549. Henrique Henriques, a Portuguese Jesuit of Jewish descent who worked on the coast from 1547 to his death at Punnaikayal in 1600, mastered Tamil, wrote the first Tamil grammar by a European and saw through the press the Thambiran Vanakkam (Quilon, 1578), the first book printed in an Indian script, followed by the Kiristiyani Vanakkam (1579) and the Flos Sanctorum (Punnaikayal, 1586). The Jesuits organised confraternities, schools and hospitals in the villages, and the statue of Our Lady of the Snows (Panimaya Matha) at Tuticorin, venerated since 1582, became the community's emblem.

Conversion did not dissolve caste — it consolidated it. The Paravar 'Jati Talaivan' (caste headman), recognised by the Portuguese, combined religious and social leadership, and Catholic festivals such as the golden-car procession of Our Lady of the Snows became expressions of Paravar identity. When the Dutch took Tuticorin in 1658 and tried to impose Calvinism, the Paravars clung to Catholicism, secretly sheltering Jesuit priests. They later became a centre of the struggle between Padroado and Propaganda jurisdictions. Today the Paravars and Mukkuvars remain overwhelmingly Catholic and form the core of the dioceses of Tuticorin, Kottar and Thiruvananthapuram's coastal parishes.

indiaMissions.title: Robert de Nobili and the Madurai mission
indiaMissions.region: Madurai and the Tamil interior (Tiruchirappalli, Salem, Marava country), later extending to Telugu and Kannada regions
indiaMissions.summary: In 1606 the Italian Jesuit Roberto de Nobili began a radical experiment in Madurai, the capital of the Nayak kingdom. Concluding that Christianity was rejected as the 'Parangi' religion of meat-eating Portuguese and low-caste fishers, he lived as a Brahmin sannyasi, learned Tamil and Sanskrit, and allowed high-caste converts to keep the sacred thread, tuft and other caste marks as civil customs. Approved by Pope Gregory XV in 1623, the method created a large interior Tamil Catholic church but also institutionalised caste within it, and the 'Malabar Rites' it spawned were condemned by Rome in 1704 and 1744.
indiaMissions.story:
Christianity had reached Madurai before de Nobili: the Portuguese Jesuit Gonçalo Fernandes Trancoso had served a small congregation of Paravars there since 1595 without winning a single local convert in over a decade. The new arrival, Roberto de Nobili (born 1577 in Montepulciano or Rome to a Tuscan noble family related to Cardinal Bellarmine), reached Goa in 1605 and Madurai in November 1606. He concluded that the obstacle was cultural: Christians were 'Parangis', identified with the beef-eating, wine-drinking Portuguese and with low-caste converts, and no respectable Tamil could join them without becoming an outcaste.

De Nobili therefore separated himself from Fernandes and the Portuguese. He took the ochre robe of a sannyasi and later the dress of a Brahmin teacher (raja-guru), ate one vegetarian meal a day cooked by a Brahmin, lived in a hut in the Brahmin quarter and called himself a Roman of noble (Kshatriya, later Brahmin) rank. With the help of a Telugu Brahmin teacher, Sivadharma, he became perhaps the first European to master Sanskrit, and he wrote some twenty works in Tamil — including the catechism Gnanopadesam, the Attuma Nirnayam (on the soul) and the Dushana Dhikkaram (refutation of calumnies) — coining a Tamil Christian vocabulary that drew on Sanskrit. In his Latin treatise Informatio de quibusdam moribus nationis Indicae (1613) he argued that the sacred thread, the kudumi tuft, sandal paste and ritual bathing were marks of caste and social rank, not religion, and could be retained by converts once purified of idolatry. His first high-caste baptisms came in 1607–09.

The experiment caused a storm. Fernandes reported in 1610 that de Nobili was compromising the faith and dividing Christians by caste; the archbishop of Goa, Cristóvão de Sá, opposed him, while his own superior, the archbishop of Cranganore Francisco Ros, and Cardinal Bellarmine defended him. After a conference at Goa in 1619, Pope Gregory XV's constitution Romanae Sedis Antistes (31 January 1623) allowed the thread and tuft provisionally, provided superstitious elements were removed. De Nobili's mission spread to Tiruchirappalli and Salem; he was imprisoned more than once by Nayak authorities, and by the 1640s he was nearly blind. He spent his last years in Jaffna and at Mylapore, where he died on 16 January 1656.

To reach lower castes without alienating high-caste converts, the Jesuits developed a two-tier ministry in 1640: alongside 'Brahmin sannyasis' such as de Nobili, missionaries like the Portuguese Balthasar da Costa lived as 'pandaraswamis', non-Brahmin ascetics who could serve Shudra and Dalit (Paraiyar, Pallar) communities. Churches were built with separate entrances or partitions for different castes. The method produced its greatest growth not among Brahmins, few of whom converted, but among Vellalar, Udaiyar and other Shudra castes and among Paraiyars in the villages of the Kaveri delta and the Marava country. The Portuguese Jesuit John de Britto, a pandaraswami, converted many in the Marava kingdom before being beheaded at Oriyur on the orders of the Sethupathi ruler in 1693. The Italian Constanzo Beschi ('Viramamunivar', 1680–1747) wrote the Tamil epic Thembavani (1726) on the life of St Joseph and grammars of literary and colloquial Tamil, and is honoured as a classic Tamil author.

The practices of the Madurai, Mysore and Carnatic missions became known in Rome as the 'Malabar Rites', parallel to the Chinese Rites controversy. Capuchin critics in Pondicherry denounced the Jesuits for omitting ceremonies in baptism that offended caste sensibilities, for allowing the thread and caste separation, and for tolerating child marriage. The papal legate Charles-Thomas Maillard de Tournon condemned these practices in 1704, and after decades of appeals Pope Benedict XIV's bull Omnium sollicitudinum (1744) prohibited most of them, although it allowed missionaries to be assigned separately to different castes. The suppression of the Society of Jesus in 1773 devastated the mission; French Jesuits revived the 'New Madurai Mission' in 1838.

De Nobili's legacy is deeply contested. Admirers see him as a pioneer of inculturation, of serious Christian engagement with Sanskrit learning and of Indian Christian theology, whose example inspired later Catholic ashrams. Critics, including many Dalit Christian theologians, argue that his accommodation of Brahmanical norms built caste into the foundations of Tamil Catholicism, where separate seating, cemeteries, festival processions and even church walls dividing Dalits from caste Christians have persisted into the twenty-first century.

indiaMissions.title: Synod of Diamper (1599) and the Coonan Cross Oath (1653)
indiaMissions.region: Central Kerala (Cochin, Udayamperoor, Angamaly, Alangad, Kaduthuruthy)
indiaMissions.summary: In June 1599 Archbishop Alexis de Menezes of Goa convened the Synod of Diamper, which cut the St Thomas Christians off from the Church of the East, condemned 'Nestorian' teaching, burned or expurgated Syriac books and imposed Latin discipline under Jesuit bishops. Half a century of resentment exploded in the Coonan Cross Oath of 3 January 1653, when thousands swore at Mattancherry never to obey the Jesuits. Rome's Carmelite envoys won most parishes back, but the remainder formed an independent church that joined the Syriac Orthodox tradition in 1665 — the origin of the lasting division between Kerala's Catholic and Orthodox Syrian Christians.
indiaMissions.story:
The Portuguese regarded the St Thomas Christians as fellow Christians tainted by 'Nestorianism' — loyalty to the Church of the East, whose theology the Council of Ephesus (431) had condemned. When the last East Syriac metropolitan, Mar Abraham, died in 1597, Alexis de Menezes, the Augustinian archbishop of Goa, saw his chance. Early in 1599 he toured the Syrian parishes with Portuguese backing, ordaining dozens of new priests to win their loyalty and pressing the archdeacon, George of the Cross, to submit. He then summoned a synod to Udayamperoor (Diamper), near Cochin, which met from 20 to 26 June 1599 with 153 priests and some 660 lay representatives.

The synod's decrees, drafted in Portuguese and read in Malayalam translation, transformed the church. It condemned Nestorius, removed the name of the 'Patriarch of Babylon' from the liturgy and required submission to the Pope and the Padroado. Syriac books judged heretical were to be surrendered and corrected or burned; the East Syriac Qurbana was revised to conform to Latin doctrine; the veneration of East Syriac saints was forbidden. Priests, who had commonly married, were required to be celibate; the Tridentine sacraments of confirmation and auricular confession were imposed; and many customs shared with Hindu neighbours — astrology, certain marriage practices and ritual pollution beliefs — were condemned, though the synod left caste distinctions largely untouched. In 1600 Rome placed the community under Latin Jesuit bishops at Angamaly, a see transferred to Cranganore in 1605, beginning with Francisco Ros (1601–1624).

For half a century the archdeacons resisted the Jesuit bishops' attempts to govern without them. Under Bishop Francisco Garcia (1641–1659) relations broke down completely. In 1652 a bishop from the Middle East named Ahatallah, who claimed to have been sent by the patriarch, arrived at Mylapore; the Portuguese seized him and shipped him to Goa, and rumours spread in Kerala that he had been drowned in Cochin harbour. On 3 January 1653 a great crowd of Thomas Christians gathered at the church of Our Lady of Life in Mattancherry. Unable all to touch the stone cross, they tied ropes to it and swore together that they would no longer obey Garcia or the Jesuits. Tradition holds that the cross bent under the strain — hence 'Coonan Cross' (koonan kurishu, the 'leaning cross'). On 22 May 1653 at Alangad twelve priests laid hands on Archdeacon Thomas (Parambil Thomas), proclaiming him bishop as Mar Thoma I.

Rome responded by sending Italian Discalced Carmelites under the authority of Propaganda Fide rather than the Portuguese Jesuits. Led by Joseph Sebastiani, they persuaded many to return to Catholic communion, arguing that Mar Thoma I's consecration was invalid. When the Dutch East India Company captured Cochin in January 1663 and expelled Catholic missionaries, Sebastiani consecrated an Indian, Parambil Chandy (Alexander de Campo), as vicar apostolic. By then 84 of the 116 communities had returned to Rome, while 32 remained with Mar Thoma I. In 1665 the Syriac Orthodox bishop Mar Gregorios Abdul Jaleel of Jerusalem arrived and recognised Mar Thoma I, and over the following century the independent party adopted the West Syriac (Antiochene) liturgy and miaphysite Christology.

The events created the enduring division of the Thomas Christians into the Pazhayakoor ('old allegiance', the Catholic Syro-Malabar Church) and the Puthenkoor ('new allegiance', the Malankara churches). The Catholic party remained under Latin bishops — Carmelites and Padroado prelates — until Rome created vicariates apostolic for them under Indian bishops in 1896 and a full hierarchy in 1923. Latinisation itself became a long-running issue: twentieth-century scholars and bishops sought to restore East Syriac elements of the liturgy, and disputes over the form of the Qurbana led to open conflict in the Archdiocese of Ernakulam-Angamaly between 2021 and 2024. On the Puthenkoor side, the question of who held authority — a Kerala metropolitan or the patriarch of Antioch — underlay the later Orthodox–Jacobite division.

indiaMissions.legacy: Diamper and the Coonan Cross Oath are the defining trauma and the defining act of resistance in Kerala Christianity. They show how a European church, backed by an empire, tried to remake an older Asian church in its own image, and how that church answered — by an oath of collective dissent that is still remembered as an assertion of Indian Christian self-determination.

indiaMissions.title: Tranquebar: Ziegenbalg, Plütschau and the first Protestant mission
indiaMissions.region: Tranquebar (Tharangambadi) in the Danish enclave on the Coromandel coast, extending to Madras, Cuddalore, Thanjavur and Tiruchirappalli
indiaMissions.summary: On 9 July 1706 two young German Lutherans trained at Halle, Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg and Heinrich Plütschau, landed at the Danish trading post of Tranquebar, sent by King Frederik IV of Denmark. They began the first organised Protestant mission in India, with a pietist emphasis on the vernacular Bible, schools, print and the study of Tamil religion. Ziegenbalg's Tamil New Testament (1714–15) was the first printed Bible translation in any Indian language, and the Tranquebar mission became the root of Tamil Lutheranism and a model for the Protestant missionary movement.
indiaMissions.story:
Denmark had held Tranquebar since 1620, with Fort Dansborg protecting a small trading settlement, but its chaplains served only Europeans. In 1705 King Frederik IV, prompted by his court chaplain Franz Julius Lütkens, resolved to send missionaries. Finding no willing Danes, Lütkens recruited two Germans from the circle of August Hermann Francke at Halle: Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg (born 1682 in Pulsnitz, Saxony) and Heinrich Plütschau (born 1677 in Mecklenburg). They sailed from Copenhagen in November 1705 and reached Tranquebar on 9 July 1706. The Danish commandant, J. S. Hassius, and the Danish East India Company saw them as troublemakers; in 1708–09 Ziegenbalg was imprisoned for four months.

Ziegenbalg set out to learn Tamil by sitting with the children of a village school, tracing letters in the sand. Within a few years he was preaching, writing and translating. The first baptisms, of five slaves of Danish households, took place on 12 May 1707, and the Jerusalem church was consecrated that August; the larger New Jerusalem Church followed in 1718. The missionaries opened schools for boys and girls — among the first in South India to teach girls to read — and a seminary for catechists and teachers. In 1712 the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge (SPCK) in London sent a printing press, and with Tamil type cast in Halle the mission printed the Tamil New Testament (1714–15) along with catechisms, hymnals and grammars. Benjamin Schultze completed the Old Testament in 1727–28.

Ziegenbalg was also a serious student of Tamil religion and society. He collected palm-leaf manuscripts, compiled the Bibliotheca Malabarica (1708), a catalogue of Tamil books, and held public dialogues with Hindu and Muslim scholars, later published in Europe. His Genealogy of the South Indian Gods (1713) was considered too sympathetic to 'heathenism' by Francke, who refused to print it; it was published only in 1867. The Halle Reports (Hallesche Berichte), published from 1710, circulated the mission's letters across Protestant Europe and inspired Count Zinzendorf, who met Ziegenbalg in 1715, and the later British missionary societies. Ziegenbalg travelled to Europe in 1714–16, where he met George I in London, before returning to Tranquebar. Worn out by work and conflict with the mission board in Copenhagen, he died on 23 February 1719 at the age of thirty-six, leaving a congregation of some 250 baptised Christians; Plütschau had returned to Europe in 1711, and Johann Ernst Gründler died in 1720.

The mission continued under Halle-trained successors for more than a century. It ordained the first Indian Lutheran pastor, Aaron, in 1733, followed by Diogo and others; extended its work to Madras (Vepery, 1726), Cuddalore (1737), Thanjavur and Tiruchirappalli; and through the SPCK became an unusual partnership between German Lutheran missionaries and the Church of England. Its most famous later missionary, Christian Friedrich Schwartz, arrived in 1750 and became a confidant of the rulers of Thanjavur. Moravian Brethren also maintained a settlement, the 'Brethren's Garden', at Tranquebar from 1760 to 1803.

The mission struggled with caste from the start. Converts came from many backgrounds, including Vellalars, Paraiyars and Pallars, and the missionaries allowed separate seating and separate communion cups for caste and Dalit Christians to avoid losing high-caste members — a compromise later attacked by evangelical missionaries and defended by the Leipzig Mission in the 'caste controversy' of the 1840s–50s. By the late eighteenth century rationalism at Halle, war and lack of funds had weakened the mission. Denmark sold Tranquebar to the British East India Company in 1845, and in 1847 the Leipzig Evangelical Lutheran Mission took over the Tamil congregations, which became the Tamil Evangelical Lutheran Church in 1919.

indiaMissions.legacy: Tranquebar was the beginning of Protestant mission in India and arguably of the modern Protestant missionary movement. Its commitments to vernacular Scripture, literacy, print, schools and serious study of Indian religion became the standard Protestant pattern, while its compromise over caste foreshadowed one of the most persistent problems of Indian Christianity.
